metadata.title: Comparing tablet and print mode of a german reading comprehension test in grade 3: Influence of test order, gender and language

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a classroom-based sample of Grade 3 students (16 classrooms) who took the GraLeV reading comprehension test in both digital (tablet app) and print modes across two periods. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey design weights (e.g., sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and the analyses are conducted with SPSS using repeated-measures MANOVA rather than survey-weighted estimation. Because no weight variable (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is mentioned, it is not possible to confirm whether results are intended to be population-representative beyond the participating classrooms. For replication with ILSA-style weighting, analysts would need to identify the original sampling frame and appropriate weight variables; however, this paper appears to be a local field study rather than an ILSA microdata analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA-style cognitive achievement Plausible Values (PVs). Instead, it reports raw subtest scores from the GraLeV reading comprehension test and uses repeated-measures MANOVA and correlations, so PV handling is not applicable. Missing-data handling is not explicitly described: teachers provided background/validity questionnaire information for 173 students, but the paper does not state whether missing teacher questionnaires were handled via deletion rules or imputation, which is a reporting gap for validity-correlation analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were Grade 3 students in 16 classrooms who took the GraLeV in Spring 2021 in two measurement periods (digital and print) with a two-week interval. Of 320 Grade 3 students initially participating, only 249 took part in both assessment periods; teachers did not provide background information for 31 of these students, leaving 218 students for the analyses reported in Tables 1–6. The analytic sample was further split by test order (print-first vs digital-first) and by subgroup (gender; L1 vs L2 learners), and teacher questionnaire data were available for 173 students for validity-correlation analyses.

main_findings.dataset_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
main_findings.target_variable: Word subtest raw score (digital vs print)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Repeated-measures MANOVA (mode effect across all subtests): F(1, 205)=43.89, p<.001, η2=.18. Word subtest: print higher than digital; Word correlation r(digital,print)=.62; Word repeated-measures MANOVA by order: F(1,205)=10.32, η2=.05.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GraLeV Grade 3 the study compared digital (tablet app) versus print modes and leveraged test order, gender, and language background (plus teacher ratings for validity) to analyze Word subtest performance, finding that Word scores were significantly higher in the print mode and that the mode effect depended on test order. This indicates that response-format differences (e.g., drag-and-drop vs drawing lines) can meaningfully shift early reading-comprehension scores, so norming and interpretation should be mode-specific and test order should be controlled in hybrid assessments.

main_findings.dataset_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
main_findings.target_variable: Sentence subtest raw score (digital vs print)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Sentence subtest: no significant mode difference (reported as exception in Results). Sentence correlation r(digital,print)=.56. Sentence repeated-measures MANOVA by order: F(1,205)=103.22, η2=.33.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GraLeV Grade 3 the study leveraged test order, gender, and language background (and teacher ratings for validity) to analyze Sentence subtest performance, finding no significant overall mode effect but a strong test-order interaction in the second measurement period. This indicates that even when average mode differences are small for some subskills, administration sequencing can still affect comparability, so hybrid test designs should explicitly counterbalance order and avoid assuming digital and print scores are interchangeable.

main_findings.dataset_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
main_findings.target_variable: Text I subtest raw score (digital vs print)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Text I subtest: print higher than digital; Text I correlation r(digital,print)=.64. Text I repeated-measures MANOVA by order: F(1,205)=42.04, η2=.17.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GraLeV Grade 3 the study leveraged test order, gender, and language background (and teacher ratings for validity) to analyze Text I performance, finding significantly higher scores in the print mode and a substantial test-order interaction. This indicates that mode effects can extend beyond single-item formats to multi-item text comprehension tasks, so educators and test developers should treat digital and print versions as distinct measurement conditions unless response formats are made more equivalent.

main_findings.dataset_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
main_findings.target_variable: Text II subtest raw score (digital vs print)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Text II subtest: print higher than digital; Text II correlation r(digital,print)=.70 (highest and only acceptable test-retest reliability cited). Text II repeated-measures MANOVA by order: F(1,205)=5.06, η2=.02.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GraLeV Grade 3 the study leveraged test order, gender, and language background (and teacher ratings for validity) to analyze Text II performance, finding significantly higher print-mode scores and the strongest digital–print correlation (r=.70). This indicates that while some subtests may show better cross-mode stability, overall score comparability still depends on response-format implementation, so separate norming and careful validity checks remain necessary for hybrid use.

main_findings.dataset_used: GraLeV (German reading comprehension) Grade 3 — digital (tablet app) vs print — Spring 2021
main_findings.target_variable: Convergent vs discriminant validity (teacher ratings correlations)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Convergent vs discriminant: Fisher’s z-test showed reading-comprehension correlations higher than math/socio-emotional (example digital: r=0.53 vs 0.43; z(173)=1.97, p<.05). Mode-specific validity differences: Word correlations higher in print (z(173)=-1.83, p<.05); Sentence and Text I higher in digital (Sentence z(173)=1.73, p<.05; Text I z(173)=3.011, p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using GraLeV Grade 3 the study leveraged teacher ratings of reading comprehension (convergent) and math/socio-emotional skills (discriminant) to evaluate validity across digital and print modes, finding that convergent validity was consistently higher than discriminant validity in both modes. This indicates that despite score-level mode differences, both versions largely measure the intended reading construct, but mode-specific response formats can still shift which subskills align most strongly with external judgments.

data.outcome_summary: This study compared tablet (digital app) versus print administration of the German reading comprehension test GraLeV for Grade 3 students in Spring 2021, using a within-student design across two measurement periods (digital and print) with test order counterbalanced across 16 classrooms. The analytic sample comprised 218 students (Germany) who completed both periods; teacher questionnaire data were available for 173 students used for validity correlations. The results showed significant overall mode effects, with print-mode scores higher for Word, Text I, and Text II, while Sentence showed no significant overall mode difference. Correlations between digital and print subtest scores were moderate to high (r≈.56 to .70), with Text II reaching the only acceptable test–retest reliability threshold cited. Gender and L1/L2 language background did not moderate the mode effect, but test order did, indicating that response-format familiarity and sequencing influence comparability. The paper uses repeated-measures MANOVA and correlations (no ML/PV framework), and missing-data handling for teacher questionnaires is not explicitly documented.
